summary:
Algeria is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the Penal Code of 1966 (Ordinance 66-156 of 8 June 1966), which ILGA records as covering both male/male and female/female relations with 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment and fines of 500-2000 Algerian dinars. The US State Department's 2023 country report gives the same range, 2 months' to 2 years' plus fines, for undefined "homosexual acts". The UK Home Office country-of-origin information report of 26 July 2026 confirms that this 1966 Penal Code remains the operative framework.

Gender transition is not addressed by a dedicated statute, but it is blocked in practice. Cairo 52 reports that Algeria has no legal framework for gender-affirming healthcare, that Penal Code articles 274 and 264 could be used against providers, and that the absence of any legal gender-recognition route means civil-status gender-marker changes are theoretically unavailable. Cairo 52 also documents arrests within the LGBT+ community under indecency provisions (articles 333, 338 and 333 bis), with little information recorded on whether those arrested were trans. Snopes rated TRUE, on 5 August 2024, the claim that Algeria prohibits medical and surgical gender-affirming care and prohibits being transgender; that rating was published alongside the debunking of a false rumour about a boxer, and the debunked rumour does not affect the legal finding.

Enforcement is documented. On 24 July 2020 police raided a private home in el-Kharoub, Constantine Province, over an alleged gay wedding and arrested 44 people, 9 women and 35 men, mostly university students; on 3 September 2020 a court sentenced 2 to prison and gave 42 suspended terms, treating party decorations and "gay appearance" as evidence. A visibly trans person is exposed to the same indecency provisions, and the evidentiary standard used in that case indicates how little conduct is required for a charge to stand.

Detention offers no trans-specific protection. The US State Department reports that prison authorities separate vulnerable persons but that LGBTQI+ detainees have no specific legal protections, and that civil society notes compounded discrimination for LGBTQI+ persons. There is no anti-discrimination protection in law, no legal gender recognition, and no visible community infrastructure; activism operates almost entirely underground.

The UK Home Office assessment is that internal relocation within Algeria is viable for gay males, but that lesbians and trans females face societal difficulties, and that refusals of asylum are rarely certifiable as clearly unfounded. Unlike Tunisia or Morocco, Algeria has no documented trans-visitor incident on record, partly because very few tourists visit and researchers have limited access; the legal exposure for a visibly trans visitor is real, but the recorded enforcement pattern is thinner than Egypt's entrapment machinery or Tunisia's 2024-25 arrest wave.
tangentialFactors:
Regional polling indicates the social environment a trans visitor enters. An Arab Barometer survey published by the BBC on 23 June 2019, with 25,000 respondents across 10 countries plus the Palestinian territories, found Algeria was the exception in which fewer than 50% accepted a woman as head of state; the same polling recorded region-wide identification as "not religious" rising from 8% to 13% since 2013.

The legal architecture is shared with neighbouring states: the same Penal Code model that ILGA recorded in 2008 is the one the 2026 UK Home Office report confirms is still in force, so the age of the statute does not indicate repeal. What distinguishes Algeria from Egypt and Tunisia is documentation volume rather than a more permissive law.

Very low tourist arrivals and restricted researcher access mean incident reporting is sparse, so an absence of recorded trans-specific cases should not be read as an absence of risk.
